prompt: When assisting a patient with ambulation who is weak on one side, the PCT should typically walk:

options.text: On the patient's weak side to provide support
Far ahead without contact
Only on the strong side never supporting the weak side
Behind by 20 feet silently

explanation: Support the weak side and use gait belt per protocol; match pace and use assistive devices ordered.

distractorExplanations.b: Abandonment risk if too far.
distractorExplanations.c: Weak side needs support.
distractorExplanations.d: Too far behind loses control.

prompt: During an 8-hour shift, Mrs. Chen takes 240 mL coffee, 180 mL juice, 240 mL broth, 120 mL gelatin, a serving of mashed potatoes, and a 400 mL cup of ice chips. She voids 650 mL. What total intake should PCT Dana record?

options.text: 780 mL total
860 mL total
980 mL total
1,180 mL total

explanation: Intake counts every fluid and every food that is liquid at room temperature, and ice chips are recorded at half their volume. 240 + 180 + 240 + 120 (gelatin) + 200 (400 ÷ 2 for ice chips) = 980 mL. Mashed potatoes are solid food, and the 650 mL void goes in the output column.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves out the ice chips entirely; ice chips are fluid intake, recorded at half their volume (400 mL of chips = 200 mL).
distractorExplanations.b: Leaves out the gelatin; gelatin, ice cream, and popsicles turn liquid at room temperature and count as fluid intake.
distractorExplanations.d: Records the ice chips at their full 400 mL; melted chips yield roughly half that volume, so only 200 mL is recorded.

prompt: When making an occupied bed, a key principle is:

options.text: Lower both side rails and raise the bed to working height, then step away to collect clean linen
Fanfold the soiled linen toward the patient and lay the clean linen on top of the dirty roll
Keep the patient covered and use side rails/safety measures while changing linen
Remove the top sheet and bath blanket first so the bottom sheet is easier to reach on each side

explanation: Dignity, warmth, and skin protection matter during occupied bedmaking. Follow facility policy on side rails and safety measures.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving rails down with the bed raised while stepping away creates a fall risk; gather linen first and stay at the bedside.
distractorExplanations.b: Clean linen must not touch soiled linen; roll soiled linen inward and keep clean linen separate to avoid cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing the top covers first exposes the patient; a bath blanket stays over the patient throughout occupied bedmaking.

prompt: Intake and output (I&O) documentation should include:

options.text: Oral fluids and urine, while IV fluids and wound drainage are recorded only on the MAR
Meal percentages, oral fluids, and estimated urine volume when the patient voids in the toilet
Oral fluids, urine, and daily weight, with emesis and liquid stool left out of output totals
Oral fluids, IV fluids as applicable, urine, and other measurable outputs per protocol

explanation: Accurate I&O informs fluid balance assessment for the care team.

distractorExplanations.a: I&O totals include IV fluids and measurable drainage; leaving them off the I&O sheet makes the fluid balance inaccurate.
distractorExplanations.b: Urine is measured with a toilet hat or graduate, not estimated; meal percentages are a nutrition record, not I&O.
distractorExplanations.c: Emesis and liquid stool are measurable outputs that belong in I&O; daily weight is recorded on a separate flow sheet.

prompt: Fowler's position is:

options.text: Head of bed elevated (commonly 45–60°) for comfort/breathing/eating
Head of bed flat with the patient on the back and knees slightly flexed
Patient lying on the left side with the right knee drawn up toward the chest
Head of bed lowered below the level of the feet to improve venous return

explanation: Semi-Fowler's is lower elevation; High-Fowler's near 90°—used for dyspnea/meals.

distractorExplanations.b: Lying flat on the back with knees flexed is dorsal recumbent/supine positioning, not the head-elevated Fowler's position.
distractorExplanations.c: Left side-lying with the upper knee flexed is Sims' position, used for enemas and rectal procedures, not Fowler's.
distractorExplanations.d: Head lower than the feet is Trendelenburg position; Fowler's raises the head of the bed instead of lowering it.

prompt: When feeding a patient at risk for aspiration, the PCT should:

options.text: Position the patient semi-reclined at 30° and alternate large bites with sips of thin liquid
Keep head elevated, offer small bites, and ensure swallowing before next bite
Offer thin liquids through a straw between bites to help the food go down faster
Lay the patient flat for 30 minutes after the meal so the food settles before activity

explanation: Aspiration precautions require positioning and pacing; report coughing/wet voice. Follow the facility's aspiration protocol and ordered diet texture.

distractorExplanations.a: Aspiration precautions need upright positioning (about 90°) and small bites; 30° with thin-liquid washes raises aspiration risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Straws and thin liquids speed flow and increase aspiration risk; follow the ordered liquid consistency and pace slowly.
distractorExplanations.d: Patients at aspiration risk stay upright for about 30 minutes after meals; lying flat promotes reflux and aspiration.

prompt: Indwelling urinary catheter care includes:

options.text: Hanging the drainage bag on the bed's side rail so it moves with the patient when rails go up
Disconnecting the catheter from the tubing to empty the bag faster when it is nearly full
Keeping the drainage bag below bladder level and peri-care without kinking tubing
Placing the drainage bag on the floor beside the bed so gravity drainage works best

explanation: Closed system and gravity drainage reduce UTI risk; never use bag for drinking water. Perform peri-care per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Bags hang on the bed frame, not side rails; raising the rail can lift the bag above the bladder and pull on the catheter.
distractorExplanations.b: The closed system stays connected; the bag is emptied through its drain spout, since breaking the junction invites infection.
distractorExplanations.d: The bag must stay below the bladder but off the floor; floor contact contaminates the bag and its drain spout.

prompt: Pressure injury prevention includes:

options.text: Massaging reddened areas over bony prominences to restore circulation
Repositioning every 4 hours and keeping the head of bed above 45° at rest
Placing a donut-shaped cushion under the sacrum to lift it off the mattress
Repositioning on schedule, skin inspection, and keeping skin clean/dry

explanation: Relieve pressure; avoid massage over reddened areas; manage moisture.

distractorExplanations.a: Massaging reddened bony prominences can deepen tissue damage; reddened areas should be offloaded and reported instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Turning is usually at least every 2 hours, and HOB above 30° increases sacral shear; 4 hours and >45° raise injury risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Donut cushions concentrate pressure on the ring edges and reduce blood flow; pressure-redistribution surfaces are preferred.

prompt: When measuring weight on a standing scale, the PCT should:

options.text: Balance/zero the scale, assist safely, and record with footwear standards per policy
Weigh the patient at a different time each day so readings reflect normal daily variation
Have the patient keep shoes and a coat on, then subtract an estimated 5 pounds afterward
Let the patient steady themselves by holding the wall rail while the reading is taken

explanation: Accurate weights guide medication and fluid decisions.

distractorExplanations.b: Daily weights use the same time, scale, and clothing; changing the time adds variation that masks true fluid changes.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracting an estimate for clothing is inaccurate; weights use consistent minimal clothing with the scale zeroed beforehand.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaning on a rail shifts weight off the scale and gives a falsely low reading; unsteady patients need a chair or bed scale.

prompt: Oral care for an unconscious patient requires:

options.text: Supine flat position, a full cup of water to rinse, and a toothbrush to clean the gums
Lateral position, suction available, and gentle mouth care to prevent aspiration
High-Fowler's position, mouthwash rinse by syringe, and mouth care once every 24 hours
Lateral position with lemon-glycerin swabs used repeatedly to keep the mucosa moist

explanation: Airway protection is critical during unconscious oral hygiene. Position and suction follow facility protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Flat positioning and pouring rinse water into an unconscious patient's mouth risk aspiration; use side-lying and minimal fluid.
distractorExplanations.c: Unconscious patients need frequent oral care (often every 2 hours) with minimal fluid; syringe rinses can be aspirated.
distractorExplanations.d: Lemon-glycerin swabs dry and irritate the mucosa and erode tooth enamel; they are discouraged for routine oral care.

prompt: When measuring a patient's weight, the PCT should:

options.text: Use whichever scale is closest each day and record the reading in the nurse's notes later
Weigh the patient after breakfast one day and before breakfast the next to average intake
Zero/balance the scale, have the patient wear similar clothing/shoes, and record accurately
Round each reading to the nearest 5 pounds so trends are easier to compare between shifts

explanation: Accurate weights guide fluid/medication decisions; technique matters. Clothing and footwear follow the facility weighing protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Serial weights require the same scale each time and prompt charting; switching scales introduces device-to-device error.
distractorExplanations.b: Weights are taken at the same time daily, usually before breakfast after voiding; alternating times distorts fluid trends.
distractorExplanations.d: Rounding to 5 pounds hides clinically important 1–2 pound fluid shifts; record the exact reading in the ordered unit.

prompt: A patient with dysphagia is at increased risk for:

options.text: Fluid overload from thickened liquids
Urinary retention after meals
Choking only on solid foods, not liquids
Aspiration during eating/drinking

explanation: Swallowing difficulty raises aspiration and pneumonia risk—follow thickened liquids/feeding precautions.

distractorExplanations.a: Thickened liquids slow swallowing to reduce aspiration; dysphagia patients are more at risk of dehydration than fluid overload.
distractorExplanations.b: Urinary retention is not linked to swallowing difficulty; the key danger of dysphagia is food or fluid entering the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Thin liquids are often the hardest to control and the most likely to be aspirated; the risk is not limited to solid foods.

prompt: Which is the safest way to identify a patient before care?

options.text: Use two identifiers (e.g., name and date of birth) and match the wristband/order
Ask 'Are you Mr. Smith?' and confirm the name on the door card before starting care
Use the room and bed number plus the patient's name as written on the whiteboard
Check the wristband name only, since the band was verified by staff at admission

explanation: Active two-identifier verification prevents wrong-patient errors.

distractorExplanations.b: Leading yes/no questions and door cards are unreliable; ask the patient to state name and DOB and check the wristband.
distractorExplanations.c: Room and bed numbers are not patient identifiers because patients move; use two person-specific identifiers like name and DOB.
distractorExplanations.d: One identifier is not enough even from a wristband; national patient safety goals require two identifiers before each task.

prompt: When making an occupied bed, the PCT should:

options.text: Keep the bed at its lowest height while working and turn the patient without asking for help
Maintain side-rail safety, keep the patient covered, and use good body mechanics
Raise both side rails while working so the patient cannot roll in either direction
Shake out the soiled sheets at the bedside to clear crumbs before rolling them up

explanation: Occupied bedmaking prioritizes safety, privacy, and ergonomics; get help for dependent patients. Covering the patient protects dignity and warmth.

distractorExplanations.a: The bed is raised to working height during care to protect your back, then lowered when finished; get help for dependent patients.
distractorExplanations.c: The far rail is up but the working-side rail is lowered while you are there; keeping both up blocks care and can act as a restraint.
distractorExplanations.d: Shaking soiled linen disperses microorganisms into the room; roll soiled linen inward, away from your uniform.

prompt: Range-of-motion exercises should be performed:

options.text: Briskly and past the point of resistance so the joint gains new range each session
Holding the limb by the muscle belly and moving several joints together for speed
As ordered, supporting joints, and stopping if pain/resistance indicates harm
Once weekly with the patient lying prone, starting at the feet and working upward

explanation: ROM is gentle and order-based; force causes injury.

distractorExplanations.a: ROM is slow and gentle and stops at resistance or pain; forcing past it can tear tissue or dislocate a joint.
distractorExplanations.b: Joints are supported above and below and moved one at a time; grabbing the muscle belly and combining joints risks injury.
distractorExplanations.d: ROM is usually done at least daily (often with bathing) with the patient supine, working head to toe; weekly prone sessions are wrong.

prompt: When a patient removes upper dentures for oral care, the PCT should:

options.text: Clean dentures over an empty sink, then store them dry in a tissue on the overbed table
Rinse the dentures under hot running water, then return them to the mouth immediately
Hold the dentures in bare hands over the sink while brushing them with regular toothpaste
Handle dentures carefully and keep them in a labeled container with water/solution

explanation: Dentures are costly and easily misplaced; labeled containers and proper solution protect the patient. Follow policy on the soaking solution, and prevent loss or breakage.

distractorExplanations.a: Clean over a towel-lined or water-filled sink to cushion drops and store in a labeled cup; tissue-wrapped dentures get thrown out.
distractorExplanations.b: Hot water can warp dentures; use cool or lukewarm water, and the mouth also needs care before the dentures go back in.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves are required, and abrasive regular toothpaste can scratch dentures; use denture cleanser over a padded sink.

prompt: Pulse oximetry is most reliably obtained when the probe is placed on:

options.text: A clean, warm, dry finger with minimal nail polish per manufacturer/protocol
The same arm as the blood pressure cuff so both readings can be taken at once
A finger with an acrylic nail, after confirming the patient's hand is resting still
The earlobe for every adult, because finger readings run several points too high

explanation: Good perfusion and skin contact improve SpO2 accuracy; follow device instructions.

distractorExplanations.b: Cuff inflation cuts off blood flow and makes SpO2 drop or read erratically; place the probe on the opposite arm.
distractorExplanations.c: Artificial and acrylic nails block the light path and cause false readings; remove them or choose another site.
distractorExplanations.d: Earlobe probes are an alternative when finger perfusion is poor, not a universal default; finger readings are not systematically high.

prompt: When assisting with a bedpan for a bed-bound patient, the PCT should:

options.text: Provide privacy, lower the head of bed flat, and leave the patient on the pan for 30 minutes
Provide privacy, position the pan under the hips, and ensure the call light is within reach
Warm the pan, roll the patient away, and place the pan at the lower back above the hips
Remove gloves after placing the pan, then handle the used pan bare-handed to save supplies

explanation: Dignity, correct placement, and access to help are basic bedpan safety principles.

distractorExplanations.a: Raise the head of bed to a sitting position for bedpan use; long periods on the pan risk skin breakdown.
distractorExplanations.c: The pan sits under the buttocks so the opening is beneath the perineum; placed at the lower back it spills and misses.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are worn when removing and emptying the pan because it holds body fluids; bare-handed handling breaks Standard Precautions.

prompt: Ice chips given to a patient should be documented in I&O as:

options.text: Output, since melted ice is excreted as urine
Not recorded, because ice chips are a solid
Intake (fluid intake) per facility protocol
Food intake, as a percentage of the meal tray

explanation: Melting ice contributes to fluid balance and must be tracked when ordered.

distractorExplanations.a: Ice chips are consumed, so they count toward intake; output covers urine, emesis, and drainage leaving the body.
distractorExplanations.b: Ice chips melt into water and count as fluid intake (often at about half their volume) even though they are served frozen.
distractorExplanations.d: Meal percentages track nutrition; ice chips belong in fluid intake on the I&O sheet, not in food intake.

prompt: When measuring height on a stadiometer, the PCT should:

options.text: Measure with shoes on and subtract one inch, reading the headpiece from below eye level
Have the patient stand with knees bent and chin down while lowering the headpiece firmly
Record the height the patient reports at admission instead of using the stadiometer
Have the patient stand straight without shoes and read the measurement at eye level

explanation: Standardized technique yields accurate anthropometric data for care planning. Follow the facility measurement protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Height is measured without shoes rather than with an estimated subtraction, and the bar is read at eye level to avoid parallax.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients stand fully upright with heels together and head level; bent knees and a lowered chin understate height.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-reported height is often inaccurate; a measured stadiometer height is required when the order or protocol calls for it.

prompt: When applying anti-embolic (TED) stockings, the PCT should:

options.text: Apply smoothly from toe upward, remove wrinkles, and follow size/order instructions
Apply after the patient has been up walking for an hour so the legs are warmed up
Fold the top band down a few inches if the stocking feels too long for the patient's leg
Choose a size by eye, pulling from the top of the thigh down to the toes to smooth it

explanation: Proper fit supports venous return; wrinkles and rolled tops can tourniquet and impair circulation. Do not roll the top down.

distractorExplanations.b: TED hose go on before rising, while legs are elevated and least swollen; after walking, the legs are already edematous.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolled or folded tops act like a tourniquet and impair circulation; report a poor fit so the correct size is obtained.
distractorExplanations.d: Stockings are sized from leg measurements and applied from the toe upward; pulling downward bunches the fabric.

prompt: When assisting with orthostatic vital signs, the PCT should:

options.text: Measure standing first, then sitting, then lying, so the lowest pressure is recorded first
Follow the ordered sequence, support the patient, and record each set promptly
Have the patient stand quickly, and recheck only if they report feeling dizzy
Take each set back-to-back within 10 seconds so position changes do not alter results

explanation: Orthostatic testing compares position changes; timing and support reduce fall risk. The usual sequence is lying, then sitting, then standing.

distractorExplanations.a: Orthostatic checks start lying (after rest) and progress to sitting and standing; reversing the order defeats the comparison.
distractorExplanations.c: The patient rises with support and each position is measured at set intervals; waiting for dizziness misses silent drops.
distractorExplanations.d: Readings are taken after about 1–3 minutes in each position; the whole point is to capture position-related change.

prompt: Oral care for a conscious patient who needs assistance includes:

options.text: Positioning flat on the back, brushing firmly with a hard brush, and rinsing with a large cup of water
Doing the brushing for the patient even when they can hold the brush, to finish care more quickly
Positioning comfortably, using appropriate supplies, and reporting bleeding, pain, or swallow difficulty
Using full-strength alcohol mouthwash undiluted and charting a refusal without telling the nurse

explanation: Assisted oral hygiene supports comfort and infection prevention; report abnormalities to the nurse.

distractorExplanations.a: Patients sit upright for oral care; flat positioning with large rinses risks aspiration, and hard, firm brushing injures gums.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients should do as much of their own care as they can to keep independence; the PCT assists only where needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol mouthwash dries and irritates oral tissue, and refusals or abnormal findings are reported to the nurse, not just charted.

prompt: After collecting a urine specimen at the bedside, labeling should occur:

options.text: At the nurses' station after collection, using the printed label from the requisition
Before collection, by pre-labeling the empty container at the bedside to save time
In the lab, where the specimen processor matches the cup with the requisition
At the bedside immediately using two identifiers per protocol before transport

explanation: Bedside labeling after collection prevents wrong-patient specimens.

distractorExplanations.a: Labeling away from the patient invites wrong-patient errors; specimens are labeled at the bedside in the patient's presence.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-labeled empty containers can end up used for the wrong patient; label after collection in front of the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: The collector, not the lab, labels the specimen; unlabeled specimens arriving in the lab are usually rejected.

prompt: When transferring a patient to a bedside commode, the PCT should:

options.text: Lock wheelchair/brake equipment, use proper body mechanics or a gait belt, and stay for safety
Place the commode at the foot of the bed facing away and have the patient walk to it unassisted
Position the commode on the patient's weaker side and pivot toward that side for balance
Lift the patient under the arms onto the commode, then step out without placing the call light

explanation: Stable equipment and assisted transfers reduce falls during toileting. Use the gait belt as indicated.

distractorExplanations.b: The commode goes beside the bed, angled toward the patient's strong side for a short pivot, with assistance as needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients transfer toward their stronger side; leading with the weak side increases fall risk during the pivot.
distractorExplanations.d: Lifting under the arms injures shoulders, and a patient left alone on a commode must have the call light within reach.

prompt: A patient who is NPO for a morning procedure asks for water, and family brought juice. The PCT should:

options.text: Give small sips of water but no juice, since clear water is allowed under NPO
Give no oral fluids, reinforce the NPO order, and notify the nurse
Offer ice chips instead of water, since ice is not counted as oral intake under NPO
Let the patient drink the juice if the procedure is more than four hours away

explanation: NPO means nothing by mouth unless a licensed clinician changes the order; PCTs do not override it or start IVs. Notify the nurse if the patient remains thirsty or distressed.

distractorExplanations.a: NPO means nothing by mouth, including water, unless the provider writes an exception such as sips with medications.
distractorExplanations.c: Ice chips melt into fluid and are oral intake; they break NPO unless the provider specifically allows them.
distractorExplanations.d: PCTs cannot shorten NPO based on timing; only the provider changes fasting orders, and the nurse should be told.

prompt: When coaching use of an incentive spirometer as ordered, the PCT should:

options.text: Have the patient exhale forcefully into the mouthpiece to raise the indicator
Encourage quick, sharp inhalations to raise the ball to the top as fast as possible
Encourage slow deep inhalations to target level and rest between attempts
Coach 10 breaths once daily with the patient lying flat to reduce fatigue

explanation: IS coaching supports lung expansion post-op; shallow panting does not achieve ordered goals. Report inability to participate to the nurse.

distractorExplanations.a: Incentive spirometers measure inhalation; blowing out into the device is a common error that does not expand the lungs.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid inhalations spike the flow indicator but do not sustain alveolar expansion; slow, deep, sustained breaths are the goal.
distractorExplanations.d: IS is typically used about 10 times every hour while awake, sitting upright; once daily lying flat is ineffective.

prompt: A patient with peripheral arterial disease has TED hose ordered but toes are cool, pale, and painful. The PCT should:

options.text: Apply the stockings as ordered, then recheck the toes within an hour and report if unchanged
Elevate the legs on pillows above heart level and apply the stockings once color improves
Massage the toes and apply a warm heating pad to restore circulation before the stockings
Do not apply or tighten the stockings; report the cool, pale, painful toes to the nurse

explanation: Arterial insufficiency can be worsened by compression; circulatory warning signs need nursing review before applying TED hose. Report immediately.

distractorExplanations.a: Cool, pale, painful toes signal arterial compromise; compression is held and reported before application, not after.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevating ischemic legs further reduces arterial flow; with PAD signs the PCT holds the stockings and notifies the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Heating pads on ischemic feet can burn tissue with poor sensation, and massage does not fix arterial insufficiency.

prompt: When preparing a bath or shower per policy, water temperature should be:

options.text: Checked with a bath thermometer or wrist test per facility protocol to avoid scalding
Set by the patient's preference alone, since they can feel what is comfortable
Tested with the PCT's fingertips after the patient is already seated in the tub
Around 115–120°F (46–49°C) so the water stays warm through the entire bath

explanation: Older adults and certain conditions increase burn risk; temperature checks are a safety standard.

distractorExplanations.b: Older adults and patients with neuropathy may not sense scalding heat; staff verify temperature with a thermometer.
distractorExplanations.c: Fingertips are less sensitive than the wrist or a thermometer, and water is checked before the patient gets in.
distractorExplanations.d: Water above about 105–110°F can scald fragile skin; 115–120°F is too hot for patient bathing.

prompt: The sequential compression device alarm shows tubing disconnected on a post-op patient. The PCT should:

options.text: Silence the alarm and turn the pump off until the nurse can reconnect it at the next round
Reconnect only per protocol/training, ensure proper fit, and report persistent alarms to the nurse
Reconnect the tubing and tighten the sleeves so that two fingers cannot fit under them
Remove the sleeves and have the patient walk instead, since ambulation replaces the SCD order

explanation: SCDs reduce DVT risk when functioning; malfunctions need prompt appropriate response and notification.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the SCD off without telling the nurse removes DVT prophylaxis for hours; report or fix per training right away.
distractorExplanations.c: SCD sleeves should allow about two fingers underneath; overtightening can impair circulation and injure skin.
distractorExplanations.d: Ambulation does not cancel an SCD order; only the provider changes it, and the nurse decides about removal.

prompt: The first step in using a fire extinguisher is often taught as:

options.text: Pull the pin (PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep)
Aim at the base of the fire (PASS step one)
Sound the alarm (RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain)
Squeeze the handle while sweeping side to side

explanation: PASS acronym guides extinguisher use; RACE guides overall fire response (Rescue/Alarm/Contain/Extinguish-Evacuate).

distractorExplanations.b: Aiming at the base is the second PASS step; the pin must be pulled first or the handle will not discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: Alarm belongs to the RACE fire-response sequence, not to operating an extinguisher; PASS begins with Pull.
distractorExplanations.d: Squeeze and Sweep are the third and fourth PASS steps; without pulling the pin first the handle will not discharge.

prompt: Hand hygiene with alcohol-based rub is appropriate when:

options.text: Hands are covered in blood without washing first
Hands are not visibly soiled and facility policy allows it
Caring for C. difficile when soap/water is required by policy and you skip washing
After using the restroom without any hand cleaning

explanation: Visible soil/certain organisms need soap and water; otherwise ABHR is often preferred for convenience/efficacy.

distractorExplanations.a: Bloody hands need soap/water washing.
distractorExplanations.c: Spore-forming organisms often need soap/water.
distractorExplanations.d: Restroom requires hygiene.

prompt: Contact precautions typically require:

options.text: A fit-tested N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room for the patient
A surgical mask within 6 feet of the patient plus gloves for direct care
Gown and gloves for contact with the patient/environment as indicated
Gloves alone, with gowns reserved for when splashes of blood are expected

explanation: MRSA/VRE-type contact precautions use gown/gloves; airborne needs respirator/room controls.

distractorExplanations.a: N95 respirators and negative pressure are airborne precautions (TB, measles); contact precautions use gown and gloves.
distractorExplanations.b: A mask within about 6 feet is the droplet-precaution rule (e.g., influenza); contact precautions require gown and gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Gowns for expected splashes is a Standard Precautions rule; contact precautions add a gown for any patient/environment contact.

prompt: A gait belt is used to:

options.text: Secure a confused patient to the chair to prevent unassisted standing
Lift a fully dependent patient from bed to chair without a mechanical lift
Pull the patient up in bed by the belt when repositioning toward the headboard
Assist transfer/ambulation safely by providing a secure hold

explanation: Gait belts aid guided assistance; restraints need orders/protocols.

distractorExplanations.a: Using a gait belt to keep a patient seated makes it a restraint, which requires a provider order and monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Dependent patients who cannot bear weight need a mechanical lift; a gait belt only guides patients who can help.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving a patient up in bed uses a lift sheet and two staff; pulling on a gait belt causes shear and injury.

prompt: When a patient is falling, the PCT should generally:

options.text: Guide the patient to the floor safely controlling the descent if possible, then call for help
Try to catch them mid-air alone with twisting back flexion
Run away without assistance
Pull their arms upward sharply

explanation: Protect the head and ease down; don't sacrifice your back with unsafe catches.

distractorExplanations.b: Unsafe catch causes dual injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Abandonment worsens outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Arm yank injures shoulders.

prompt: Sharps should be disposed of in:

options.text: Red biohazard bags for infectious waste
Puncture-resistant sharps containers
Recapped, then placed in the regular trash
Any rigid container once it is filled to the top

explanation: Never recap with two hands; fill only to fill line.

distractorExplanations.a: Red bags are for soft blood-soaked waste; needles can puncture bags, so sharps go in rigid puncture-resistant containers.
distractorExplanations.c: Needles are not recapped by hand and do not go in regular trash; they go directly into a sharps container.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharps containers are approved puncture-resistant units replaced at the fill line (about three-quarters full); overfilling causes sticks.

prompt: Restraint use requires:

options.text: A family member's written consent and a check on the patient at least once per shift
A nurse's verbal approval and tying the restraint to the side rail with a quick-release knot
A provider order (except true emergencies per policy) and frequent monitoring/documentation
A provider order renewed weekly and release of the restraint for toileting every 8 hours

explanation: Restraints are last resort; monitor skin, toileting, circulation, and attempt alternatives.

distractorExplanations.a: Restraints need a provider order, not family consent, and are checked far more often than once per shift.
distractorExplanations.b: Restraints are tied to the bed frame, not side rails, which move and can injure; a provider order is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Restraint orders are renewed far more often than weekly, and release for toileting and skin care is about every 2 hours.

prompt: The most effective way to prevent spread of pathogens between patients is:

options.text: Wearing the same gloves for all patients all day
Shaking linen into the air
Leaving bedpans uncleaned
Hand hygiene and correct PPE use

explanation: Hand hygiene is #1; change gloves between patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Glove reuse spreads pathogens.
distractorExplanations.b: Aerosolizing linen spreads microbes.
distractorExplanations.c: Dirty equipment contaminates.

prompt: RACE in fire safety stands for:

options.text: Rescue, Alarm, Confine/Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate
Run, Argue, Cry, Exit
Remove All Care Equipment first always before patients
Radio, Assess, Coffee, Eat

explanation: Prioritize people, alarm, contain smoke/fire, then extinguish if small/safe or evacuate.

distractorExplanations.b: Silly mnemonic.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients before equipment.
distractorExplanations.d: Not a break mnemonic.

prompt: Standard Precautions apply to:

options.text: Patients with a confirmed bloodborne infection
All patients, regardless of known infection status
Patients on contact, droplet, or airborne isolation
Any patient with visible blood or open wounds

explanation: Assume blood/body fluids are potentially infectious for everyone.

distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions are not limited to known HIV/HBV/HCV cases; infection status is often unknown, so they apply to everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Isolation categories are Transmission-Based Precautions layered on top of Standard Precautions, which apply to every patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions apply before blood is visible; any patient's blood, body fluids, or non-intact skin may be infectious.

prompt: The PCT finds a frayed electrical cord on a device. The correct action is:

options.text: Wrap the frayed area with electrical tape and report it at the end of the shift
Keep using it if it passes a quick power-on test, then note it in the shift report
Remove it from service, tag/report per policy, and do not use until repaired
Unplug it by pulling the cord and move it to the patient's bathroom for storage

explanation: Damaged cords are fire/shock hazards—out of service until fixed.

distractorExplanations.a: Tape is not an approved repair; a damaged cord is a shock and fire hazard, so the device leaves service immediately.
distractorExplanations.b: Powering on does not prove the insulation is intact; frayed cords are removed from service until biomed repairs them.
distractorExplanations.d: Pull the plug, not the cord, and do not store electrical equipment in wet areas; tag it and send it for repair.

prompt: Which is correct about bed alarms for fall-risk patients?

options.text: They replace hourly rounding once activated, so checks can be spaced out
They let staff leave the bed in high position since the alarm will sound
They count as a restraint, so a provider order is needed before use
They are adjuncts—respond promptly and continue other fall precautions

explanation: Alarms support but do not replace comprehensive fall prevention.

distractorExplanations.a: Bed alarms alert staff after a patient moves; they do not replace hourly rounding, toileting, and other fall precautions.
distractorExplanations.b: The bed stays in the lowest position with brakes locked; an alarm sounds only after the patient is already getting up.
distractorExplanations.c: Bed alarms do not restrict movement, so they are not restraints and do not require a restraint order.

prompt: PCT Jordan is leaving the room of a patient on contact and droplet precautions, wearing gloves, a gown, a surgical mask, and a face shield. Which removal sequence follows CDC guidance?

options.text: Gloves, face shield, gown, mask, then hand hygiene
Mask, face shield, gown, gloves, then hand hygiene
Face shield, gloves, mask, gown, then hand hygiene
Gloves, mask, gown, face shield, then hand hygiene if soiled

explanation: CDC's doffing sequence removes the most contaminated items first: gloves, then the face shield by its band, then the gown rolled inside-out, then the mask by its ties, with hand hygiene right after. Touching face items with soiled gloves, or removing the mask early, risks contaminating the face.

distractorExplanations.b: Removing the mask and face shield first means still-contaminated gloves touch the face; gloves are the dirtiest item and come off first.
distractorExplanations.c: Handling the face shield with soiled gloves contaminates the face area, and the gown comes off before the mask, which is removed last.
distractorExplanations.d: The mask comes off last, after the gown and face shield, and hand hygiene is required after every PPE removal, not just when hands look soiled.

prompt: Proper use of a gait belt includes:

options.text: Applying loosely at the chest over the gown so the patient can breathe comfortably
Applying snugly at the waist over clothing and holding the belt to guide/support
Applying snugly at the waist and lifting a dependent patient by the belt alone
Applying at the waist directly on bare skin and holding it with a fingertip grip

explanation: Gait belts aid safe ambulation/transfers with proper technique and adequate assistance. Do not lift heavy dependent patients by the belt alone without help.

distractorExplanations.a: Gait belts go snugly around the waist, not loosely at the chest; a loose belt slides up and gives no secure hold.
distractorExplanations.c: The belt guides patients who can bear weight; fully dependent patients need a mechanical lift and more staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Belts go over clothing to protect the skin, and staff use a firm underhand grip on the belt for a secure hold.

prompt: Which PPE sequence concept is correct after caring for a patient on contact precautions?

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, and skip hand hygiene if the hands look clean
Remove PPE in the hallway after leaving the room so the room stays uncontaminated
Remove contaminated PPE carefully to avoid self-contamination, then perform hand hygiene
Use alcohol gel on gloved hands and keep the same gloves on for the next patient

explanation: PPE removal order and hand hygiene prevent self-contamination and spread.

distractorExplanations.a: Hand hygiene is required after PPE removal even when hands look clean, because gloves can have micro-tears.
distractorExplanations.b: PPE for contact precautions is removed at the doorway before leaving so contaminated items stay inside the room.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves are single-use and changed between patients; sanitizing gloved hands does not make the gloves safe to reuse.

prompt: Oxygen is in use in a patient's room. The PCT must enforce:

options.text: No smoking within the room, though e-cigarettes are permitted at the bedside
Petroleum jelly on the lips and nostrils to prevent dryness from the cannula
Wool blankets in place of cotton to keep the patient warm during oxygen use
No smoking, sparks, or open flames near oxygen sources per policy

explanation: Oxygen supports combustion; ignition sources create fire/explosion risk.

distractorExplanations.a: E-cigarettes and vape devices are ignition sources too; they are prohibited wherever oxygen is in use.
distractorExplanations.b: Petroleum-based products are flammable in oxygen-rich air; use water-based lubricants for dry lips and nares.
distractorExplanations.c: Wool and synthetics generate static sparks; cotton is preferred around oxygen to reduce ignition risk.

prompt: The PCT finds a wet floor near the nurses' station. The first action is to:

options.text: Block/warn the area, post a wet-floor sign, and notify environmental services
Finish current patient care first, then return later to post a wet-floor sign
Wipe it with a dry towel and let it air-dry, with no sign posted afterward
Write an incident report first and then let housekeeping decide when to clean it

explanation: Immediate warning prevents slips; proper cleanup follows facility protocol. Notify environmental services or other appropriate staff.

distractorExplanations.b: A wet floor is an immediate slip hazard; warn people right away rather than leaving it unmarked while you finish tasks.
distractorExplanations.c: Even after wiping, the area stays slippery until dry and must be marked; the spill source may also be biohazardous.
distractorExplanations.d: Incident reports document events after the hazard is controlled; first warn others and get the spill cleaned.

prompt: Before transferring a patient into a wheelchair, the PCT should:

options.text: Position the chair at the foot of the bed facing away and leave the brakes unlocked
Lock the wheelchair brakes and remove or swing footrests aside as appropriate
Leave the footrests down so the patient can step onto them while pivoting
Place the chair on the patient's weaker side so the strong leg leads the pivot

explanation: Locked brakes and clear foot placement prevent falls during pivot transfers.

distractorExplanations.a: The chair goes beside the bed at about 45° on the strong side with brakes locked; unlocked brakes let it roll.
distractorExplanations.c: Stepping on footrests tips the chair forward; footrests are swung away before the transfer and replaced after.
distractorExplanations.d: The wheelchair goes on the patient's stronger side so they pivot toward it with the strong leg bearing weight.

prompt: Contaminated dressings and blood-soaked materials should go in:

options.text: A puncture-resistant sharps container along with used needles and lancets
A regular trash bag, double-bagged and taped to contain any leaking fluid
A red biohazard bag or designated infectious waste container per policy
The soiled linen hamper so laundry can process them with contaminated sheets

explanation: Biohazard containers prevent exposure and comply with regulated medical waste handling.

distractorExplanations.a: Sharps containers are for items that can puncture; soft blood-soaked dressings go in red biohazard bags.
distractorExplanations.b: Double-bagging regular trash does not meet regulated medical waste rules; saturated items go in red biohazard bags.
distractorExplanations.d: Dressings are disposable waste, not linen; putting them in the hamper exposes laundry staff to blood.

prompt: After a needlestick with a used needle, the PCT should first:

options.text: Squeeze the puncture to make it bleed, apply bleach, and report it at the end of the shift
Wash the site with soap and water, then wait to report it until any symptoms develop
Report it to the nurse first, then wash the site once the source patient is tested
Wash the area with soap and water and report immediately per occupational exposure protocol

explanation: Prompt washing and reporting enable source testing and prophylaxis per policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing and bleach are not recommended, and delayed reporting can miss the time window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
distractorExplanations.b: Washing is right, but exposures are reported immediately; HIV PEP works best within hours, not after symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: The wound is washed first and immediately; waiting for source testing leaves contaminated blood in the wound.

prompt: After caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile, hand hygiene should be:

options.text: Soap-and-water washing; alcohol-based rub is not reliable against C. diff spores
Alcohol-based hand rub, since it kills C. diff spores faster than soap and water
Glove removal followed by alcohol rub, as gloves already blocked the spores
Washing with a bleach wipe on bare hands to kill spores on the skin

explanation: C. diff spores are not reliably killed by alcohol gel; wash with soap and water after care even if hands do not look soiled.

distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol does not kill C. diff spores; mechanical soap-and-water washing physically removes them.
distractorExplanations.c: Spores can contaminate hands during glove removal; soap-and-water washing is required after C. diff care.
distractorExplanations.d: Bleach wipes are surface disinfectants and harm skin; hands are washed with soap and water after C. diff care.

prompt: Droplet precautions (e.g., influenza) typically require a mask when:

options.text: Only when performing aerosol-generating procedures such as suctioning
On entering the patient's room, keeping it on while inside the room
Upon entering a negative-pressure room, using a fit-tested N95 respirator
When the patient is actively coughing, and not during quiet bedside care

explanation: Under CDC droplet precautions, staff put on a surgical or procedure mask when entering the patient's room and wear it while inside, because droplets from talking, coughing, or sneezing can reach anyone in the room. N95 respirators and negative-pressure rooms belong to airborne precautions for diseases such as TB and measles.

distractorExplanations.a: Droplet precautions call for a mask on room entry for any care; aerosol-generating procedures add airborne-level protection on top.
distractorExplanations.c: Negative-pressure rooms and N95 respirators are airborne precautions (TB, measles), not droplet precautions for influenza.
distractorExplanations.d: Droplets also spread from talking and sneezing, so the mask goes on at room entry, not only when the patient coughs.

prompt: A small blood spill on the floor should be managed by:

options.text: Wiping it up with a dry paper towel while gloved, then letting the floor air-dry
Pouring disinfectant directly on the blood and mopping it immediately without gloves
Donning PPE, containing the spill with absorbent material, disinfecting per protocol
Covering it with a towel and waiting for housekeeping, with no warning sign posted

explanation: Blood is OPIM under Standard Precautions; PPE and disinfectant reduce exposure risk. Dispose of the waste properly afterward.

distractorExplanations.a: Wiping without disinfectant leaves bloodborne pathogens behind; after absorbing, apply an EPA-registered disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are required for any blood contact, and disinfectant needs its full contact time before the area is wiped.
distractorExplanations.d: A blood spill needs prompt PPE cleanup or a posted warning and notification; an unmarked covered spill exposes others.

prompt: When delivering a meal tray to a patient on contact precautions, the PCT should:

options.text: Enter without PPE since meal delivery involves no direct contact with the patient
Return the used tray to the shared meal cart with the other patients' trays
Hand the tray in through the doorway and ask the patient to set it on the bed
Follow isolation protocol for entry/exit and handle tray as contaminated

explanation: Isolation diets/trays stay in the room or follow designated workflow to prevent cross-contamination. Leave or remove items per policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Contact precautions require gown and gloves when entering and touching the environment, including the overbed table.
distractorExplanations.b: Trays from contact-precautions rooms follow a designated workflow; mixing them with other trays spreads organisms.
distractorExplanations.c: Dependent patients need setup help, and isolation does not cancel meal assistance; don PPE and set up the tray.

prompt: When bagging soiled linen, the PCT should:

options.text: Hold away from the body without shaking and roll/contain in the bag
Shake the linen gently over the trash to remove crumbs before bagging it
Carry the bundle against your uniform to keep it from dropping on the floor
Place it on the floor in the room until the hamper is brought to the door

explanation: Shaking aerosolizes pathogens; minimal handling and hand hygiene protect staff and environment. Perform hand hygiene before touching anything else.

distractorExplanations.b: Any shaking of soiled linen disperses microorganisms; roll it inward and bag it without shaking.
distractorExplanations.c: Soiled linen is held away from the uniform; contact transfers organisms to your clothes and the next patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Soiled linen does not go on the floor, which contaminates the environment; bag it directly at the bedside.

prompt: When donning PPE for contact isolation before entering the room, a common sequence is:

options.text: Gloves first, then gown, then mask, so hands are protected while tying the gown
Gown first, then mask/eye protection if needed, then gloves with cuffs over the gown
Mask first, then gloves, then gown with the gown cuffs pulled over the gloves
Gown, gloves, then mask, adjusting the mask's nose clip with the gloved hands

explanation: Gown-then-gloves overlap prevents wrist exposure during contact care.

distractorExplanations.a: CDC donning order is gown, mask, eye protection, then gloves last so the glove cuffs cover the gown sleeves.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves go on last with cuffs over the gown sleeves; gown cuffs over gloves leave a gap at the wrist.
distractorExplanations.d: Adjusting a mask with gloved hands contaminates it; mask and eyewear go on before gloves.

prompt: To reduce tripping hazards from oxygen tubing, the PCT should:

options.text: Run tubing across the doorway where staff can easily see it
Tape tubing flat to the floor across the patient's path
Route tubing behind furniture, coiled safely off the floor
Cut the extra tubing to shorten it and reconnect it with tape

explanation: Proper routing and equipment checks reduce fall risk for patients and staff. Report excessive tubing length to the nurse.

distractorExplanations.a: Tubing across a walkway is a trip hazard even when visible; route it along walls or behind furniture.
distractorExplanations.b: Taped tubing in a walking path still catches feet and can kink; keep it coiled off the floor instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Altering oxygen tubing can leak and interrupt flow; excess length is reported so the nurse can replace it.

prompt: A patient on airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis requires:

options.text: A surgical mask for staff within 6 feet of the patient and a private room with the door left open
A fit-tested N95 respirator and a positive-pressure room so air is pushed outward
Gown and gloves for contact, with a surgical mask worn by staff during suctioning
A fit-tested N95 (or equivalent) respirator and a negative-pressure room with the door kept closed

explanation: Airborne isolation uses respirators and engineered ventilation controls to contain small particles.

distractorExplanations.a: Surgical masks within 6 feet are droplet precautions; TB requires fit-tested N95s and a closed negative-pressure room.
distractorExplanations.b: Positive pressure is for protective isolation of immunocompromised patients; TB rooms are negative pressure to keep air in.
distractorExplanations.c: Gown and gloves are contact precautions; TB is airborne and requires an N95 respirator at every room entry.

prompt: Environmental cleaning for C. difficile contamination often requires:

options.text: EPA-registered sporicidal disinfectant (e.g., bleach-based per policy)
Alcohol-based wipes on high-touch surfaces, as for routine room cleaning
Quaternary ammonium disinfectant, the standard choice for MRSA rooms
Hand hygiene gel spread on bed rails and tables after the patient leaves

explanation: Spores survive routine alcohol cleaning; sporicidal agents are used on surfaces per protocol. Alcohol rub alone is not adequate on surfaces.

distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol does not kill C. diff spores on surfaces; a sporicidal agent such as bleach is required.
distractorExplanations.c: Quats work for MRSA but are not sporicidal; C. diff rooms need a sporicidal product such as bleach.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand gel is not a surface disinfectant and alcohol cannot kill spores; use an EPA-registered sporicidal product.

prompt: After venipuncture, the safest way to handle the used needle is to:

options.text: Recap it with both hands, then carry it to the sharps container at the nurses' station
Activate the safety device immediately and place it in a sharps container
Unscrew the needle from the holder by hand and drop just the needle in the sharps box
Set it on the tray and activate the safety device after bandaging the patient's arm

explanation: Two-handed recapping is a classic needlestick risk; engage the safety feature and discard in a puncture-resistant container. Do not recap with two hands.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-handed recapping is a leading cause of needlesticks; activate the safety device and use the point-of-use container.
distractorExplanations.c: Needles are not unscrewed by hand; the whole holder-needle unit goes into the sharps container in one piece.
distractorExplanations.d: The safety device is engaged immediately after withdrawal; setting an exposed needle down risks a stick.

prompt: The correct patient identification process before a draw/EKG includes:

options.text: Using two identifiers (e.g., name and DOB) matching the order/wristband
Asking 'Are you Ms. Lee?' and confirming the room and bed on the order
Checking the name on the wristband against the bed card on the wall
Using the name and room number from the requisition, compared with the chart

explanation: Two identifiers prevent wrong-patient procedures.

distractorExplanations.b: Leading questions and room numbers are unreliable; the patient states name and DOB, matched to the wristband.
distractorExplanations.c: A bed card is not a valid identifier and a single name check is one identifier; use two matched to the order.
distractorExplanations.d: Room number is not a patient identifier, and matching paperwork to paperwork without the patient misses wrong-patient errors.

prompt: Lavender EDTA tubes are commonly used for:

options.text: Coagulation PT/INR as first choice
CBC/hematology testing
Glucose gray-top exclusively as the EDTA use
Blood cultures as the primary bottle type

explanation: EDTA preserves cellular elements for CBC; coag uses citrate; gray for glucose glycolysis inhibition; cultures use special bottles.

distractorExplanations.a: Coag is light blue citrate.
distractorExplanations.c: Gray is fluoride.
distractorExplanations.d: Cultures are bottles/SPS.

prompt: After needle removal, activate safety and apply pressure to:

options.text: Increase arterial spurting
Eliminate the need for labeling
Prevent hematoma and stop bleeding
Cause hemoconcentration intentionally

explanation: Adequate pressure/time reduces bruising; label at bedside.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure stops bleeding.
distractorExplanations.b: Labeling still required.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemoconcentration is a preanalytical error.

prompt: For a routine 12-lead EKG, V4 is placed at:

options.text: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, anterior axillary line
Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line

explanation: Know V1–V6 landmarks; limb leads on limbs (or torso per protocol when needed).

distractorExplanations.a: The 4th ICS at the right sternal border is V1; V4 sits lower and more lateral at the 5th ICS midclavicular line.
distractorExplanations.b: The 5th ICS anterior axillary line is V5; V4 is at the midclavicular line on the same horizontal level.
distractorExplanations.c: The 4th ICS at the left sternal border is V2; V4 is at the 5th ICS in the left midclavicular line.

prompt: Artifact from patient shivering on EKG is reduced by:

options.text: Warming the patient and ensuring relaxed muscles/good electrode contact
Turning on the 60-Hz filter, since shivering is a type of electrical interference
Asking the patient to grip the bed rails firmly to keep the arms still
Increasing the gain to 20 mm/mV so the waveforms stand out from the artifact

explanation: Somatic tremor creates fuzzy baseline; comfort helps.

distractorExplanations.b: The 60-Hz filter targets AC electrical interference; somatic tremor from shivering is reduced by warming and relaxation.
distractorExplanations.c: Gripping tenses the muscles and increases somatic artifact; the arms should rest relaxed at the patient's sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubling the gain enlarges the artifact along with the complexes; it does not remove muscle tremor.

prompt: Order of draw is intended to prevent:

options.text: Hemolysis from slow tube filling
Additive carryover between tubes
Clotting in the lavender EDTA tube
Hemoconcentration from the tourniquet

explanation: Follow CLSI order; invert tubes gently to mix additives.

distractorExplanations.a: Hemolysis comes from technique (small needles, shaking); order of draw prevents additive cross-contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Clotting in EDTA tubes is prevented by prompt gentle inversion, not by the sequence in which tubes are filled.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemoconcentration is caused by leaving the tourniquet on longer than about 1 minute, not by tube sequence.

prompt: A tourniquet left on too long may cause:

options.text: Hemodilution and falsely decreased protein levels
Clotting in the needle and a falsely low platelet count
Hemoconcentration and falsely elevated analytes
Glycolysis and falsely decreased glucose results

explanation: Limit tourniquet time (~1 minute) before access.

distractorExplanations.a: Prolonged venous stasis concentrates proteins and cells; it causes hemoconcentration, not dilution.
distractorExplanations.b: Tourniquet time affects analyte concentration; clotting in the needle relates to slow fills and poor technique.
distractorExplanations.d: Falsely low glucose comes from delayed processing (glycolysis), not tourniquet time; stasis raises analytes.

prompt: If a patient is allergic to adhesive, for EKG the PCT should:

options.text: Apply standard electrodes but remove them within 5 minutes of the tracing
Postpone the EKG until the provider changes the order to a rhythm strip
Apply a thin layer of lotion under each electrode to protect the skin
Use alternative electrodes/skins preps per policy and document allergy

explanation: Allergy adaptations maintain test quality and skin integrity.

distractorExplanations.a: Even short contact can trigger an adhesive reaction; hypoallergenic electrodes are used for allergic patients.
distractorExplanations.b: An allergy does not change the test ordered; adapt the electrodes per policy and notify the nurse if unsure.
distractorExplanations.c: Lotion under electrodes blocks conduction and causes artifact; it does not prevent an adhesive reaction.

prompt: Capillary puncture in adults is often performed on:

options.text: The side of the middle or ring finger
The thumb tip always preferred
The index finger tip center exclusively as best practice
The palm center

explanation: Avoid thumb/index often due to callus/use; use lateral fingertip pulp.

distractorExplanations.b: Thumb more callused.
distractorExplanations.c: Index often avoided.
distractorExplanations.d: Palm not standard capillary site.

prompt: Syncope during phlebotomy: first actions include:

options.text: Finish filling the current tube quickly, then remove the needle and tourniquet
Stop the draw and protect the patient from injury (lower head/supine)
Have the patient sit up straight and take deep breaths before continuing
Apply an ammonia inhalant right away to keep the patient awake for the draw

explanation: Safety first; notify nurse/provider as needed.

distractorExplanations.a: At the first sign of syncope the tourniquet and needle come out immediately; continuing risks injury if the patient falls.
distractorExplanations.c: Sitting upright worsens cerebral blood flow during fainting; lower the head or lay the patient down.
distractorExplanations.d: Ammonia inhalants are discouraged in many policies because of airway risk; stop the draw and position safely.

prompt: Before performing a capillary glucose check, the PCT should:

options.text: Verify the order, identify the patient, and squeeze the finger hard to get a large drop
Clean the fingertip with alcohol and puncture right away, before the alcohol has dried
Verify the order/protocol, identify the patient, and ensure the meter/strips are in date
Choose the center of the index finger pad and run quality control once a month

explanation: POCT accuracy and safety depend on ID, valid supplies, and skin prep; lancets are single-use. Meter and strips must also be appropriate for the test.

distractorExplanations.a: Squeezing ('milking') the finger adds tissue fluid and hemolysis, falsely changing glucose; let blood flow freely.
distractorExplanations.b: Wet alcohol dilutes the sample and stings; let the site air-dry completely before the puncture.
distractorExplanations.d: Punctures go on the side of the fingertip pad of the middle or ring finger; QC is run daily or per manufacturer.

prompt: Which ECG artifact is commonly caused by patient shivering?

options.text: Exact 60-cycle flatline only from good contact
Normal PQRST with perfect baseline
Printer paper jam
Somatic tremor artifact

explanation: Muscle tremor creates irregular fine artifact; warm/support the patient and ensure contact.

distractorExplanations.a: 60-cycle is electrical interference pattern.
distractorExplanations.b: Tremor is not a normal tracing.
distractorExplanations.c: Paper jams are mechanical.

prompt: When collecting a urine specimen for culture, the PCT should instruct the patient (clean-catch) to:

options.text: Cleanse as directed, void a small amount, then collect midstream into a sterile container
Collect the first part of the stream into the sterile cup, then finish in the toilet
Cleanse as directed, then pour the first morning void from a clean bedpan into a cup
Void the midstream portion into a clean, non-sterile cup and cap it within the hour

explanation: Midstream clean-catch into a sterile container reduces contamination.

distractorExplanations.b: First-stream urine flushes urethral bacteria; culture specimens use the midstream portion to avoid contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Bedpan urine is non-sterile; culture specimens are collected midstream directly into the sterile container.
distractorExplanations.d: Culture specimens need a sterile container; a clean non-sterile cup can introduce bacteria and false growth.

prompt: A PCT notices the IV site is swollen, cool, and pale with pain. The PCT should:

options.text: Apply a warm compress and elevate the arm, then report it at the next scheduled round
Leave the IV line and rate untouched and report the findings to the nurse at once
Clamp the IV tubing and remove the tape to inspect the insertion site more closely
Lower the IV bag below the site to check for blood return before telling the nurse

explanation: Swelling, coolness, pallor, and pain at an IV site suggest infiltration. The PCT does not manipulate the IV, change the rate, or apply treatments; they leave the line as it is and notify the nurse immediately so the nurse can assess, stop the infusion, and decide on care.

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing warm or cold compresses is a nursing decision after assessment, and infiltration needs immediate reporting.
distractorExplanations.c: Clamping lines and handling IV dressings are outside PCT scope; report the swollen, cool site to the nurse right away.
distractorExplanations.d: Checking for blood return is a nursing assessment; PCTs do not manipulate IV lines and report infiltration signs first.

prompt: For a routine 12-lead ECG, V4 is placed at:

options.text: Fourth intercostal space right sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, midaxillary line (left)
Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line (left)
Midway between V2 and V4 on the left chest

explanation: V4 is 5th ICS MCL; V1 is 4th ICS right sternal border.

distractorExplanations.a: That is V1.
distractorExplanations.b: The 5th ICS midaxillary line is V6; V4 is at the midclavicular line on the same horizontal level.
distractorExplanations.d: The point midway between V2 and V4 is V3; V4 itself sits at the 5th ICS in the left midclavicular line.

prompt: Blood collection tubes must be gently inverted after fill to:

options.text: Speed clotting by shaking the tube firmly 10 times
Release trapped air so the tube fills to the line
Separate serum from cells before centrifugation
Mix additive with blood without causing hemolysis

explanation: Gentle inversion ensures anticoagulant mixes; rough shaking hemolyzes samples.

distractorExplanations.a: Shaking hemolyzes red cells; even clot-activator tubes are inverted gently, about 5 times, not shaken.
distractorExplanations.b: Fill volume is set by the tube's vacuum; inversion mixes the additive and does not change the fill level.
distractorExplanations.c: Separation happens during centrifugation after clotting; inversion only mixes the additive with the blood.

prompt: A patient has an IV infusing in the right arm and a usable vein in the left arm. For venipuncture the PCT should typically:

options.text: Draw from the left (non-IV) arm to avoid diluted or contaminated specimens
Draw immediately above the running IV without notifying the nurse
Disconnect the IV independently to use that vein first
Use the IV catheter hub as a routine blood-draw port without training or policy

explanation: Blood drawn above a running IV can be diluted or contaminated; prefer the opposite arm and stay within PCT scope.

distractorExplanations.b: Drawing above an infusing IV skews results.
distractorExplanations.c: PCTs do not discontinue IVs independently.
distractorExplanations.d: IV-hub draws require specific authorization/training.

prompt: For a standard 12-lead ECG, chest lead V1 is placed at the:

options.text: Fifth intercostal space at the left midaxillary line
Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border
Second intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
Over the xiphoid process

explanation: V1 is right parasternal 4th ICS; other leads have distinct landmarks.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes V6 region.
distractorExplanations.c: That is not a standard V1/V2 landmark pairing.
distractorExplanations.d: Xiphoid is lower than V1.

prompt: Before applying ECG electrodes, the skin should be:

options.text: Coated with a thin layer of lotion to improve conduction under each pad
Shaved over every electrode site on all patients before applying the pads
Cleaned of oils/lotion and dried to improve adhesion and reduce artifact
Wiped with alcohol and the electrodes applied while the skin is still wet

explanation: Dry, clean skin improves contact; excess moisture or oil increases artifact.

distractorExplanations.a: Lotion increases impedance and lifts electrodes; skin should be clean and dry, not moisturized.
distractorExplanations.b: Hair is clipped where it prevents contact, not shaved routinely on every patient; shaving causes nicks and irritation.
distractorExplanations.d: Alcohol must dry fully before electrodes go on; wet skin reduces adhesion and causes artifact.

prompt: Standard ECG paper speed is typically:

options.text: 5 mm/s, used for routine rhythm strips at the bedside
10 mm/s, matching the standard 10 mm/mV gain setting
12.5 mm/s unless a faster speed is specifically ordered
25 mm/s unless a different speed is specifically ordered

explanation: 25 mm/s is the routine default; 50 mm/s doubles time calibration.

distractorExplanations.a: 5 mm/s is not a standard recording speed; routine 12-leads and rhythm strips run at 25 mm/s.
distractorExplanations.b: 10 mm/mV is the standard gain (amplitude) calibration, not the paper speed; routine speed is 25 mm/s.
distractorExplanations.c: 12.5 mm/s is a rarely used half-speed option; the routine default is 25 mm/s, with 50 mm/s for fast rates.

prompt: The basilic vein is often considered a last-choice draw site because it:

options.text: Lies close to arteries and nerves, increasing injury risk
Is the most superficial vein and collapses easily
Lies on the lateral thumb side, where hematomas form most
Contains valves that cause hemolysis in most tubes

explanation: Medial antecubital basilic proximity to the brachial artery/nerve favors cephalic/median preference. The risk is highest in inexperienced hands.

distractorExplanations.b: The median cubital is the most superficial, well-anchored vein; the basilic is avoided for its nerve and artery proximity.
distractorExplanations.c: The lateral (thumb-side) vein is the cephalic, a second choice; the basilic is medial, near the brachial artery.
distractorExplanations.d: Valves can impede flow but do not cause hemolysis in tubes; the basilic is last choice because of nearby nerves and artery.

prompt: Heel stick capillary collection on an infant should be performed:

options.text: On the central back curve of the heel, after warming, using a 2.4 mm adult lancet
Only per facility protocol/training, using appropriate lancet depth/site and warming
On the medial or lateral heel, squeezing firmly and continuously to speed blood flow
On the side of the middle fingertip, as for adults, after warming the infant's hand

explanation: Neonatal/infant capillary draws follow strict site, depth, and warming protocols to prevent injury.

distractorExplanations.a: The posterior heel curvature overlies bone; punctures go on the medial or lateral plantar surface with depth of 2.0 mm or less.
distractorExplanations.c: The site is right, but constant firm squeezing causes hemolysis and tissue-fluid contamination; use gentle intermittent pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Infant fingersticks risk hitting bone; infants under about 1 year get heel sticks, not fingersticks.

prompt: Fist pumping before venipuncture can cause:

options.text: Hemodilution, falsely lowering potassium and calcium results
Faster clotting that prevents adequate tube fill volume
Hemolysis and hemoconcentration, falsely affecting some results
Vein collapse, so a smaller butterfly needle becomes required

explanation: Repeated pumping increases hemolysis and can alter analytes; gentle warm-up only if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Fist pumping concentrates the sample and releases potassium from muscle; it raises potassium rather than diluting it.
distractorExplanations.b: Fist pumping alters analyte levels through muscle activity and hemolysis; it does not cause clotting that blocks tube fill.
distractorExplanations.d: Vein collapse comes from excessive vacuum or small veins, not pumping; pumping's main effect is falsely raised potassium.

prompt: If the first venipuncture attempt fails, the PCT should:

options.text: Redirect the needle sideways under the skin to find the vein
Keep the tourniquet on and try again in the same arm right away
Make up to four more attempts before notifying the nurse
Release tourniquet, apply pressure, and follow facility policy

explanation: Patient safety limits attempts; escalation prevents excessive trauma and syncope. Policy often allows one more attempt by trained staff before escalating.

distractorExplanations.a: Lateral probing can injure nerves and arteries; only slight forward or back adjustment is allowed, then release.
distractorExplanations.b: The tourniquet is released after a failed attempt; leaving it on beyond 1 minute causes hemoconcentration.
distractorExplanations.c: Most policies allow two attempts per collector before escalating; four more attempts traumatizes the patient.

prompt: Reversing the right arm (RA) and left arm (LA) limb electrodes will typically show:

options.text: Inverted deflections in limb leads (e.g., swapped P/QRS direction) on the tracing
Inverted complexes in V1 and V2 with normal limb leads throughout the tracing
Low-voltage, flat complexes in the chest leads with 60-cycle interference lines
A wandering baseline in each lead that rises and falls with the patient's breathing

explanation: Limb lead reversal swaps polarity and inverts complexes in affected leads.

distractorExplanations.b: Limb electrode swaps change the limb leads (lead I inverts); precordial V1–V2 are unaffected by RA/LA reversal.
distractorExplanations.c: 60-cycle interference is electrical artifact; RA/LA reversal inverts the P wave and QRS in lead I.
distractorExplanations.d: Baseline wander with breathing is respiratory artifact from poor contact, not limb-electrode reversal.

prompt: Chest lead V6 is placed at the:

options.text: Fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (left side)
Fifth intercostal space in the midaxillary line (left side)
Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line (left side)

explanation: V6 is lateral at 5th ICS MAL; know progression from V1–V6.

distractorExplanations.a: The 5th ICS anterior axillary line is V5; V6 is further lateral at the midaxillary line on the same level.
distractorExplanations.c: The 4th ICS at the left sternal border is V2; V6 is lateral at the 5th ICS midaxillary line.
distractorExplanations.d: The 5th ICS midclavicular line is V4; V6 sits two landmarks lateral at the midaxillary line.

prompt: A wandering baseline on ECG that tracks respirations is often caused by:

options.text: 60-cycle AC interference from nearby electrical equipment
Somatic tremor from muscle tension or shivering in the patient's arms and legs
Respiratory movement altering electrode contact (respiratory artifact)
Limb lead reversal between the right and left arm electrodes

explanation: Rhythmic baseline drift with breathing suggests motion/contact artifact; ensure secure electrodes.

distractorExplanations.a: AC interference produces a thick, regular fuzzy baseline, not a slow wave that follows breathing.
distractorExplanations.b: Muscle tremor gives an irregular jagged baseline; slow drift tied to respirations is wandering-baseline artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: Lead reversal inverts complexes in lead I; it does not make the baseline rise and fall with breathing.

prompt: A lavender-top tube arrives at the lab marked QNS (quantity not sufficient). The PCT should:

options.text: Pour blood from an overfilled tube of a different color into it until it reaches the fill line
Ask the lab to run the test anyway since EDTA tubes do not need a full draw
Draw a second lavender tube and combine both partial tubes into one sample
Report the event, document per policy, and recollect if ordered—QNS may reject testing

explanation: Underfilled EDTA tubes may be rejected; proper fill to the mark prevents QNS.

distractorExplanations.a: Transferring blood between tubes carries additive contamination and wrong ratios; QNS samples are recollected.
distractorExplanations.b: Underfilled EDTA tubes have excess anticoagulant that distorts cell counts; QNS samples are often rejected.
distractorExplanations.c: Pooling tubes mixes volumes and additive ratios and breaks labeling rules; collect a properly filled new tube.

prompt: When a patient has a bilateral arm amputation, limb ECG electrodes may be placed:

options.text: On the torso/shoulder area per facility protocol to approximate limb lead positions
On the chest lead positions V1 and V6, reusing those electrodes for the limb leads
On the stumps at different heights on each side so the leads can be told apart
On the lower legs as usual, leaving the arm leads disconnected during recording

explanation: Modified torso placement is a recognized adaptation when arms are unavailable.

distractorExplanations.b: Chest leads need their own electrodes; limb electrodes go on the shoulders or upper torso per protocol.
distractorExplanations.c: Placement on stumps must be symmetrical in height on both sides; asymmetric sites distort the limb-lead axis.
distractorExplanations.d: Disconnected arm leads leave leads I, II, III, aVR, and aVL blank; arm electrodes move to the upper torso instead.

prompt: A rhythm strip suddenly looks flat in one lead while the patient is talking and alert. The PCT should:

options.text: Call a code for asystole and start chest compressions right away
Check electrode contact and lead connections and notify the nurse
Switch the monitor to a different lead and continue without reporting
Increase the gain on that lead until the complexes become visible again

explanation: A talking patient is not in asystole; loose leads mimic a flat line. PCTs troubleshoot connections and report—they do not interpret 12-leads for treatment. Do not diagnose asystole or start treatment.

distractorExplanations.a: An alert, talking patient has a pulse and is not in asystole; a flat lead is a contact problem, not cardiac arrest.
distractorExplanations.c: Changing leads may help view the rhythm, but a lead-off problem still needs fixing and reporting to the nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising gain on a disconnected lead shows nothing; the cause is a loose electrode or wire to recheck.

prompt: A PCT is asked to perform a task outside their training/facility scope. They should:

options.text: Refuse politely and inform the nurse/supervisor so it can be reassigned
Perform it under a coworker's guidance if the coworker has done it before
Complete it carefully this one time, then request training afterward
Delegate it to another PCT on the unit who is less busy right now

explanation: Stay within scope; patient safety requires trained personnel.

distractorExplanations.b: A coworker's experience does not expand the PCT's scope; tasks outside training are reassigned by the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Doing an untrained task even once risks patient harm and violates scope; training must come before performing it.
