distractorExplanations.d: PCTs do not delegate tasks; the nurse assigns work, and the other PCT may also lack the needed training.

prompt: HIPAA requires PCTs to:

options.text: Access any chart on the unit as long as it is not shared outside
Access only the minimum necessary PHI for their job duties
Share PHI with family members who visit the patient
Obtain written consent before sharing PHI with the care team

explanation: Curiosity viewing and gossip are violations.

distractorExplanations.a: Access must be job-related; viewing charts of patients not in your care is a breach even if nothing is shared.
distractorExplanations.c: Family receives PHI only with patient permission or per policy; visiting the patient does not authorize disclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA permits sharing PHI for treatment among the care team without separate written patient consent.

prompt: Therapeutic communication includes:

options.text: Belittling fears
False reassurance that 'nothing is wrong' when symptoms exist
Open-ended questions, empathy, and clarifying without judging
Interrupting constantly

explanation: Support emotional safety while gathering accurate information.

distractorExplanations.a: Belittling harms trust.
distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance blocks reporting.
distractorExplanations.d: Interruptions block expression.

prompt: During 0800 vitals, PCT Marco gets 188/112 mm Hg on Mr. Patel, who reports a new headache. Mr. Patel's assigned RN is off the unit and has not answered two pages. What should Marco do?

options.text: Recheck it in 30 minutes and report it then if still high
Page the physician directly and ask for a PRN medication
Chart the reading and report it at the end-of-shift handoff
Report it to the charge nurse now, noting the headache

explanation: A PCT reports abnormal findings up the chain of command: the assigned nurse first and, if that nurse cannot be reached, the charge nurse right away. A BP of 188/112 with a new headache can signal a hypertensive emergency, so waiting is unsafe, and going straight to the physician bypasses the nurse.

distractorExplanations.a: Delays reporting a possibly dangerous reading with a new symptom; abnormal vitals with symptoms are reported right away, not after a wait.
distractorExplanations.b: Skips the nursing chain of command and requests a medication, which is outside PCT scope; the nurse assesses and contacts the provider.
distractorExplanations.c: Charting alone is not reporting; a critical reading with a new headache cannot wait hours for the shift handoff.

prompt: Cultural sensitivity includes:

options.text: Respecting beliefs/preferences and using interpreters when language barriers exist
Using a patient's bilingual child to interpret medical details to save time
Applying the same care routine to every patient so no group is treated differently
Assuming a patient's food and care preferences based on their ethnic background

explanation: Qualified interpreters beat family translation for clinical accuracy when possible.

distractorExplanations.b: Family members, especially children, are not qualified medical interpreters; use a trained interpreter.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal treatment does not mean identical care; cultural sensitivity adapts care to individual beliefs and needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Stereotyping by ethnicity is a cultural competence error; ask each patient about personal preferences.

prompt: If you make a documentation error, you should:

options.text: Erase the entry neatly and rewrite it so the record looks clean and legible
Correct per facility policy (e.g., single line, initial, date)
Black out the error with a marker so it cannot be misread, then initial it
Write the correction in the margin without initials so it does not draw attention

explanation: Legal records must show transparent corrections. Do not erase or obliterate the original entry.

distractorExplanations.a: Erasing obliterates the original entry and looks like tampering; draw a single line, initial, and date.
distractorExplanations.c: Blacking out hides the original text; corrections must leave the original readable under a single line.
distractorExplanations.d: Corrections must be dated and initialed to show who made them and when; unsigned margin edits are improper.

prompt: Patient rights include:

options.text: Access to their own chart directly from the PCT on request at any time
Choosing which staff member is assigned to them on every shift
Privacy, respectful care, and involvement in care decisions as applicable
Receiving any treatment they request, even if the provider has not ordered it

explanation: Rights come with responsibilities; staff also deserve safety.

distractorExplanations.a: Patients access records through the facility's formal process, not by the PCT handing over the chart.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients can raise concerns about caregivers, but they do not have a right to choose staff assignments.
distractorExplanations.d: Patients may refuse treatment, but they cannot demand treatments a provider has not ordered or judged appropriate.

prompt: A conflict with a coworker should be handled by:

options.text: Reporting directly to human resources first, before speaking with the coworker
Raising it during shift report in front of the whole team so everyone hears both sides
Avoiding the coworker and asking the charge nurse to change your assignments
Addressing privately and professionally, then involving supervisor if unresolved/safety issue

explanation: Professional conflict resolution protects teamwork and patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Most minor conflicts start with a private conversation; HR is escalation for unresolved or serious issues.
distractorExplanations.b: Public discussion during report embarrasses staff and distracts from patient handoff; address it privately.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoidance leaves the conflict unresolved and can affect patient care; talk to the coworker first.

prompt: Incident reports are used to:

options.text: Document unusual events for quality improvement and risk management
Record disciplinary action against the staff member involved in the event
Replace the clinical note so the event is not mentioned in the patient chart
Notify the patient's family and insurer of every staff error in writing

explanation: Follow facility policy on what goes in chart vs incident system. Incident reports are not typically filed in the patient chart as a progress-note substitute.

distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are non-punitive tools for finding system problems, not disciplinary records.
distractorExplanations.c: The chart still records the facts and care given; the incident report is filed separately, not as a substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Incident reports are internal, confidential QI documents; disclosure to families follows a separate process.

prompt: Professional appearance and punctuality matter because they:

options.text: Are required by HIPAA as part of the privacy rule
Support patient trust, infection control, and team reliability
Determine eligibility for NHA certification renewal
Mainly affect how patients rate the hospital food service

explanation: Uniforms, ID badges, and short nails often relate to safety policies.

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA governs the privacy of health information; dress codes and attendance come from facility policy.
distractorExplanations.c: NHA renewal depends on continuing education credits and fees, not workplace appearance or punctuality.
distractorExplanations.d: Appearance and punctuality affect trust, safety, and staffing coverage, not food-service satisfaction.

prompt: A visitor asks for details about a patient's diagnosis. The PCT should:

options.text: Share the diagnosis if the visitor can correctly state the patient's full date of birth
Give a general summary of the diagnosis without using medical terms
Decline to share PHI and direct them to the appropriate authorized process/nurse
Ask the visitor to sign the visitor log, then share the diagnosis

explanation: PHI disclosure requires authorization/care-team need-to-know.

distractorExplanations.a: Knowing a DOB does not prove authorization; disclosure depends on the patient's consent or an approved process.
distractorExplanations.b: A plain-language summary is still PHI disclosure; PCTs do not explain diagnoses to unauthorized visitors.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing in for visitation does not authorize PHI access; refer to the nurse and the patient's wishes.

prompt: Which behavior demonstrates professional boundaries?

options.text: Accepting small gifts quietly so the patient's family does not feel rejected
Sharing your personal phone number so the patient can reach you after discharge
Friending patients on social media to support them after they go home
Keeping relationships therapeutic and not exchanging romantic advances with patients

explanation: Boundaries protect patients and staff; dual relationships and social media PHI are prohibited.

distractorExplanations.a: Gifts are handled per facility policy, usually declined or reported; secret acceptance blurs boundaries.
distractorExplanations.b: Personal contact after discharge creates a dual relationship; patients use the facility's channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Social media connections with patients cross professional boundaries and risk PHI exposure.

prompt: If the PCT makes a documentation error, the correct approach is:

options.text: Correct it according to facility policy (e.g., amendment) without erasing the original
Rewrite the whole page from memory and shred the original so the record is neat
Ask the nurse to delete the electronic entry and re-enter it under your login
Add a late entry backdated to the original time so the timeline looks correct

explanation: Transparent corrections maintain legal integrity of the record.

distractorExplanations.b: Destroying the original and recreating the page is falsification; the original must stay in the record.
distractorExplanations.c: EHR entries are amended with an audit trail, not deleted; deleting removes legal evidence of the original.
distractorExplanations.d: Late entries carry the actual current date and time and are labeled late; backdating is falsification.

prompt: Team communication using SBAR typically includes:

options.text: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan in a progress note
Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation/Request
Symptoms, Baseline, Allergies, and Response to treatment
Safety, Behavior, Activity, and Rest observations for the shift

explanation: SBAR structures clear handoffs and escalation.

distractorExplanations.a: Subjective/Objective/Assessment/Plan is SOAP charting, not the SBAR verbal communication format.
distractorExplanations.c: In SBAR the B is Background and the A is Assessment; Symptoms/Baseline/Allergies/Response is not the SBAR structure.
distractorExplanations.d: SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; it is a communication format, not an observation checklist.

prompt: Workplace violence from a threatening visitor should lead the PCT to:

options.text: Calm the visitor alone in a private room away from other patients
Restrain the visitor physically until security arrives on the unit
Prioritize safety, remove self/patients from harm, and call security
Finish care for the current patient, then report it at the end of shift

explanation: Safety systems and de-escalation/security response protect everyone. Follow the facility's violence-response procedure.

distractorExplanations.a: De-escalating in an isolated room removes help and exits; stay in view of others near an exit and call security.
distractorExplanations.b: Staff should not physically restrain visitors; trained security or police manage threats while staff stay safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Credible threats need an immediate security response; waiting until end of shift leaves everyone at risk.

prompt: If a PCT suspects elder abuse based on inconsistent injuries and statements, they should:

options.text: Ask the family member directly about the injuries before deciding to report
Wait until there is clear proof of abuse before making any report
Document the injuries in the chart and bring them up at next week's care plan conference
Report to the nurse/supervisor and follow mandated reporter and facility policy promptly

explanation: Healthcare workers are mandated reporters in many jurisdictions; timely reporting protects vulnerable patients.

distractorExplanations.a: Questioning the suspected abuser can endanger the patient; report suspicions without investigating yourself.
distractorExplanations.b: Mandated reporters report reasonable suspicion; proof is not required and investigators determine the facts.
distractorExplanations.c: Charting is needed, but suspected abuse must be reported promptly, not held for a later conference.

prompt: Posting a patient photo on personal social media without authorization is:

options.text: A HIPAA violation and unprofessional conduct subject to discipline
Acceptable if the patient's face is blurred or cropped out
Permitted when the patient gives verbal permission at the bedside
Allowed if the account is private and limited to close friends

explanation: Any identifiable PHI in social posts breaches privacy rules.

distractorExplanations.b: Tattoos, rooms, wristbands, or context can still identify the patient; blurring does not make the post permissible.
distractorExplanations.c: Disclosure needs written authorization under facility policy, and personal social media posting is usually prohibited anyway.
distractorExplanations.d: Private accounts still disclose PHI to people without a need to know; privacy settings do not cure the breach.

prompt: A patient offers the PCT cash for extra favors. The PCT should:

options.text: Accept it but donate the cash to the unit's staff fund afterward
Politely decline and report the gift per facility policy
Accept small amounts under $20 since nominal gifts are allowed
Decline the cash but provide the extra favors to keep the patient happy

explanation: Gifts can create undue influence and boundary violations; follow policy on declining/reporting. Declining and reporting maintains professional boundaries.

distractorExplanations.a: Accepting cash for favors still creates an obligation; donating it later does not fix the boundary problem.
distractorExplanations.c: Some policies allow token non-cash gifts, but cash offered for extra favors is declined and reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Preferential care for one patient is itself a boundary problem; care follows the plan, and the offer is reported.

prompt: A family member asks the PCT to explain the physician's diagnosis in detail in another language. The PCT should:

options.text: Explain the diagnosis simply using the patient's discharge paperwork
Translate if the PCT is fluent, since fluency qualifies as interpreting
Not independently explain or translate the diagnosis; notify the nurse
Ask the patient's bilingual teenager to translate the physician's notes

explanation: Explaining a diagnosis is a licensed-clinician task. PCTs escalate and use qualified interpreters for role-appropriate talk—they do not ad-lib medical translations. Use a qualified interpreter only for communication within the PCT role.

distractorExplanations.a: Explaining a diagnosis is a licensed clinician task even with paperwork in hand; the PCT notifies the nurse.
distractorExplanations.b: Fluency is not interpreter qualification; medical interpreting requires trained, qualified interpreters.
distractorExplanations.d: Family members, especially minors, are not qualified medical interpreters and may omit or distort information.

prompt: When a competent patient insists on leaving against medical advice (AMA), the PCT should:

options.text: Call security to keep the patient on the unit until the physician arrives to approve it
Help the patient pack and walk them out, since competent adults may leave at any time
Have the patient sign the AMA form with the PCT as witness, then notify the nurse
Notify the nurse immediately so AMA process, education, and documentation can occur

explanation: AMA workflows are nursing/provider responsibilities; PCTs escalate promptly. Follow facility AMA policy.

distractorExplanations.a: A competent adult can leave AMA; holding them with security without legal grounds is false imprisonment.
distractorExplanations.b: Competent patients can leave, but the nurse must be told first so AMA education and the form are completed.
distractorExplanations.c: The AMA discussion and form are handled by the nurse or provider; the PCT notifies the nurse before any form.

prompt: A provider calls and tells the PCT to give a patient an extra dose of pain medication. The PCT should:

options.text: Not accept or carry out the verbal medication order; notify the nurse
Write down the order, read it back, and give it to the nurse to carry out
Accept the order since the provider gave it directly, then tell the nurse
Give the dose if it is already in the patient's medication drawer

explanation: PCTs do not take verbal medication orders, administer meds, or prescribe. Licensed nurses receive and transcribe orders. A licensed nurse receives the order.

distractorExplanations.b: Read-back is how licensed nurses take verbal orders; PCTs do not receive medication orders at all.
distractorExplanations.c: A direct call from the provider does not make the PCT a licensed receiver of medication orders.
distractorExplanations.d: Medication administration is outside PCT scope whatever is stocked; the nurse receives and gives the dose.

prompt: A patient asks the PCT whether today's EKG or lab results mean they are having a heart attack. The PCT should:

options.text: Explain the EKG findings briefly since the PCT recorded the tracing
Not diagnose or interpret results for treatment; notify the nurse
Reassure the patient that the results look normal so they stay calm
Tell the patient to ask the doctor tomorrow and continue with other tasks

explanation: Result interpretation and treatment changes are licensed-clinician duties. PCTs report the question and any distress—they do not diagnose. Stay with the patient if they are distressed.

distractorExplanations.a: Recording an EKG does not authorize interpretation; explaining results belongs to the nurse or provider.
distractorExplanations.c: Saying results are normal is still interpretation and may be false reassurance; refer the question to the nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: A patient worried about a heart attack needs the nurse notified now; delaying may miss real cardiac symptoms.

prompt: Clocking in for a coworker who is not present (buddy punching) is:

options.text: Acceptable if the coworker is in the parking lot and arrives soon
A minor policy issue handled by a verbal reminder from HR
Time fraud and grounds for disciplinary action including termination
Allowed if the charge nurse approves it during short staffing

explanation: Accurate time records are legal and payroll requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Any punch for someone not present falsifies time records; being nearby does not change that.
distractorExplanations.b: Buddy punching is payroll fraud, typically leading to serious discipline or termination, not just a reminder.
distractorExplanations.d: No supervisor can authorize falsified time records; late arrivals are documented accurately.

prompt: If a patient has an advance directive in the chart, the PCT should:

options.text: Follow the family's verbal wishes when they differ from the written directive
Explain the directive's meaning to the patient when they ask about it
Help the patient update the directive by writing in their new wishes
Know where it is documented and report questions or changes to the nurse

explanation: Advance directives guide licensed providers; PCTs support locating and communicating concerns. Do not interpret legal wishes independently.

distractorExplanations.a: Family disagreements are referred to the nurse or provider; the PCT does not override the written directive.
distractorExplanations.b: Explaining a legal and medical directive is beyond PCT scope; questions go to the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Changes to advance directives require a formal legal process; PCTs report requests to the nurse.

prompt: When floated to an unfamiliar unit, the PCT should:

options.text: Receive orientation to equipment, assignments, and emergency procedures
Follow the home unit's procedures, since policies are standard across units
Accept each task assigned, since float staff cannot decline assignments
Review only the patient list and skip the emergency equipment locations

explanation: Orientation reduces errors; unfamiliar procedures require supervision. Ask questions before accepting unfamiliar tasks.

distractorExplanations.b: Units differ in equipment, layouts, and protocols; a floated PCT needs the receiving unit's orientation.
distractorExplanations.c: Float staff can and should decline tasks outside their training and inform the charge nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: Knowing crash cart, exit, and alarm locations is a core part of float orientation, not an optional step.

prompt: If a coworker makes sexually harassing comments, the PCT should:

options.text: Wait to report until the harassment happens at least three more times
Document objectively and report through HR/supervisor per facility anti-harassment policy
Confront the coworker publicly at the nurses' station so others see the behavior stop
Report it to the state nursing board rather than to the facility's HR department

explanation: Workplace harassment policies require reporting; retaliation and normalization are harmful.

distractorExplanations.a: Harassment should be reported when it occurs; policies do not require a pattern of repeated incidents.
distractorExplanations.c: Public confrontation can escalate conflict; use the formal reporting channel through supervisor or HR.
distractorExplanations.d: Workplace harassment goes through the facility's policy channel (supervisor/HR), not a licensing board.

prompt: During electronic health record downtime, the PCT should:

options.text: Hold charting until the system is restored, then enter it from memory
Record care on personal notes and phone photos to upload later
Follow the facility downtime plan for paper documentation and orders
Use the paper forms and shred them once the system is back online

explanation: Downtime plans maintain continuity and legal record integrity. The plan also covers medication workflows.

distractorExplanations.a: Delayed charting from memory loses accuracy; downtime plans use paper forms in real time.
distractorExplanations.b: Personal notes and phone photos of PHI are not approved records and risk privacy breaches.
distractorExplanations.d: Downtime paper records are scanned or entered and retained per policy; shredding destroys the legal record.

prompt: A patient asks the PCT to witness their handwritten will at the bedside. The PCT should:

options.text: Sign as a witness after reading the will
Ask another PCT to sign as the witness
Have the patient's roommate witness it
Decline politely and notify the nurse

explanation: Legal witnessing has specific requirements and is not a nursing assistant duty. Witnessing legal documents is outside PCT scope and policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Witnessing legal documents is outside the PCT role and policy; reading the will first does not make it appropriate.
distractorExplanations.b: Passing the request to another PCT does not fix the problem; facility policy routes it through the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Arranging witnesses is not the PCT's role, and involving a roommate exposes the patient's private information.

prompt: The PCT believes staffing is unsafe for assigned acuity. The appropriate action is:

options.text: Report concerns through chain of command and document objectively
Refuse the assignment and leave the unit after telling the charge nurse
Post about the unsafe staffing on social media to pressure management
Call the state health department before telling the charge nurse

explanation: Advocacy uses proper channels; abandonment worsens safety. Do not abandon patients while concerns are addressed.

distractorExplanations.b: Leaving after accepting an assignment is patient abandonment; report concerns while continuing care.
distractorExplanations.c: Public posts bypass the chain of command and risk exposing patient or facility information.
distractorExplanations.d: External reporting is a later step; concerns start with the charge nurse and the chain of command.

prompt: A nurse asks the PCT to sign a chart entry for care the PCT did not perform. The PCT should:

options.text: Sign it, since the nurse is responsible for any entry made under the nurse's direction
Refuse to falsify documentation and report the request to supervision per policy
Sign only if the nurse confirms the care was done by someone else
Refuse to sign but keep the request to yourself to avoid conflict

explanation: Only document care actually provided; falsification is fraud and patient safety risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Each person is accountable for their own signature; signing for care not performed is falsification.
distractorExplanations.c: Documentation reflects care you personally performed; you cannot sign for another person's work.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusing is right, but a request to falsify records must also be reported to supervision.
